newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian financial group attacks war bonds plan.
newsitem.headline: Colombian financial group attacks war bonds plan.

text.p: A group of leading financiers on Sunday attacked the Colombian government's plans to issue bonds to fund its anti-guerrilla war, saying the measure could undermine an already weak economy.

The National Association of Financial Institutions urged the government in a radio interview to consider alternatives to its proposed war bonds, by speeding up the privatization of state-owned industries or by seeking loans abroad.

"War bonds in such a weak economy could cause an enormous, additional damage. We do not believe in these bonds and we think the government could find other ways to give this money to defense," said association chairman Armando Montenegro, in an interview with RCN radio.

Faced with a rising spiral of guerrilla violence, President Ernesto Samper's administration is looking to raise an additional $420 million to $600 million dollars for the 1997 defense budget with the war bonds.

If congress approves the move, individuals or businesses with a net worth of more than $85,000 would be required to purchase the five-year bonds, which would be issued in denominations of 500,000 pesos ($480) and carry a 6 percent annual interest rate.
A previous plan to levy a one-off war tax on the rich was dropped after Colobia's Constitutional Court ruled it unconstitutional.

Montenegro told RCN radio on Sunday that the bonds would merely push the government deeper into debt and become an additional obstacle in an economy which showed just 2.2 percent growth in gross domestic product in the second quarter of this year -- the lowest level this decade.

He argued foreign loans could be negotiated on more favorable terms. Montenegro also suggested the government could squeeze additional military spending out of its 1997 budget by reordering priorities or free up funds for a counterinsurgency campaign by stepping up the pace of privatization of state-controlled enterprises.

In the last two weeks, more than 120 people have been killed in one of the bloodiest rebel offensives in decades, leading some military experts to suggest the armed forces have lost control of the situation.

In a speech to the representatives of the metallurgical industry this weekend, army commander Gen. Harold Bedoya said he lacked the manpower and equipment to fight the guerrillas effectively, one of Colombia's leading dailies, El Espectador, reported on Sunday.
Bedoya said he needed to triple the size of the army -- from 120,000 soldiers to a 360,000-strong force -- and insisted on the need for more helicopters to transport ground troops to conflict zones.
